Learning Objectives
Review examples of the manner in which health care during a disaster is different from health
care during non-disaster times.
Explain different types of disasters and when a disaster transitions to a mass casualty incident.
Describe how to prepare for disasters and mass casualty incidents.
Discuss examples of the role of the orthopaedic surgeon in disasters and mass casualty
incidents.
Introduction
Disasters can be natural or man-made.

A mass casualty incident (MCI) is defined as “an overwhelming event, which generates more
patients at a time than locally available resources can manage using routine procedures.”
Protocols and preparation are major keys to success during a disaster or MCI.
Overview
Orthopaedic injuries are common in all disasters, and all orthopaedic surgeons should
understand how to respond to the orthopaedic injuries and the disaster.
A disaster can be natural or man-made, and its effects may be felt locally, nationally, and
worldwide.
A MCI occurs if a disaster overwhelms local resources and special procedures are necessary to
coordinate disaster response.
Success during a disaster is predicated on preparation before the disaster occurs.

Overview
Orthopaedic injuries represent a high percentage of the trauma observed during
disasters and MCIs.1,2 Therefore, orthopaedic surgeons must understand disasters and
disaster response and be prepared to act appropriately. A disaster can be defined as “a
sudden calamitous event bringing great damage, loss, or destruction.”3 Disasters are
classified as natural (eg, hurricanes, tornadoes, earthquakes) or man-made (eg, mass
shootings, bombings, terrorist attacks, industrial catastrophes, mass transportation
crashes).4 The effect of devastation dispensed by a disaster may be local, national, or
worldwide. The duration of disaster effects may be short-lived or sustained for years.
A MCI occurs if the acute effect of a disaster “generates more patients at a time than
locally available resources can manage using routine procedures.”5 In MCIs, specialized
protocols exist for the triage of patients, management of first responders, and allocation
of equipment to ensure maximal patient benefit with the use of scarce resources. MCI
protocols have been successfully used in response to many man-made disasters, such
the Boston Marathon bombing, and natural disasters, such as Hurricane Katrina.6 Many
aspects of MCI protocols have been adapted to help healthcare providers during the
COVID-19 pandemic.7

The preparatory events that occur before a disaster contribute to the success of MCI
protocols.4,5 An example that illustrates this principle is the mass shooting in San
Bernardino, California. A review of the two hospitals involved in the response to this
shooting showed that their success in managing the situation was credited to
preparedness through practicing established protocols.8 Rehearsals allowed for quick
mobilization of resources and coordination of patient care between the first responders
and two university health systems (Resource 1). Disasters and MCIs can cause extensive
damage, with short- and long-term consequences. Understanding the causes of these
disasters, the process of preparation, and the role of orthopaedic surgeons in the
response may lead to successful management and recovery.
Structured Disaster Preparation and Response
Preparation and practice are the most important steps to ease the effects of a disaster.
Disaster planning occurs in four stages: mitigation, preparation, response, and rehabilitation.
The Incident Command System (ICS) is used to ensure appropriate response to the disaster
and resource use.

Structured Disaster Preparation and Response
Predicting the type and timing of each disaster is impossible. Geography, demographics,
and an understanding of local industry may help predict the disasters that may or may
not affect a certain area (ie, hurricanes are unlikely to occur in Minnesota); however,
warnings with regard to when a disaster will strike ranges from no warning to days.
Therefore, preparing, planning, and practicing protocols for disasters are the most
important steps in easing the effects of a disaster. The all-hazards approach is used and
allows for a uniform, flexible, and scalable method to meet various disaster scenarios in
every community9 (Resource 2).
Guidelines for disaster preparedness have divided the process into four phases:
mitigation, preparation, response, and rehabilitation4 (Resource 3; Figure 1; Table 1).

In the mitigation phase of disaster planning, the goal is to use interventions that will
prevent or reduce the likelihood of a disaster happening, or if a disaster happens,
interventions from this phase will reduce the effects of the disaster. Mitigation
involves the use of experiences from previous disasters, and the process of mitigation
occurs before and after a disaster. Examples of mitigation include building
modifications to withstand hurricane-force winds, security screening at large events,
and strategic placement of dams/drainage pipes to minimize flooding.
In the preparation phase, the goal is to tell a person or team what to do in the event
of an emergency. The preparation phase occurs before the disaster strikes. Examples
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:55 PM
AAOS | Disaster and Mass Casualty Preparedness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000591
5/17

of preparation include participating in drills, stockpiling water/food, and building
tornado shelters. A review of disasters and mass casualty events revealed that
preparation is the phase that is credited with saving many lives. In the hospital setting,
preparation may include coordinating patient flow, designating care teams, and
stockpiling supplies.
In the response phase, the goal is to take actions to save lives, such as going to a
tornado shelter during a tornado or turning off the electric grid during a wildfire. The
Federal Emergency Management Agency defines the response phase as putting the
plans developed in the preparedness phase into action. In contrast to the mitigation
phase, these are the actions to take during an emergency to prevent death and
destruction. To ensure that the response phase goes as planned, an ICS is established
to oversee the disaster response.
The final phase of disaster planning is rehabilitation. The goal of this phase is to
return to a safer situation and, eventually, a version of normal. Examples of actions
taken during the rehabilitation phase are rebuilding and inspection of buildings,
reconnection of utilities, and counseling for those affected. The recovery phase occurs
after the threat of the disaster has resolved and serves a springboard for discussion
about interventions to mitigate damage from future disasters.
Preparation for the disaster will have no substantial effect unless that plan can be
executed. To ensure the disaster response plan is executed, each disaster must establish
an ICS.10 The concept of the ICS was developed in the 1970s and has served as a reliable
framework to structure the disaster response. Despite the perceived rigidity of the ICS, it
allows for customizability and scalability for the disaster at hand. The command staff
consists of the incident commander and section chiefs for operations, planning, logistics,
and finance. In addition, individual officers are responsible for public information, safety,
and liaison. The incident commander is the individual ultimately in charge of the disaster
response and usually is a person who is familiar with the type of disaster at hand and
the various roles that comprise the ICS. The incident commander is not required to have
a medical background but should have a grasp of how to manage multiple facets of a
disaster. Under the command staff are the general staff who help manage the resources,
finances, public information (to communicate with the community and media), and
front-line medical personnel. Orthopaedic surgeons involved in disaster response at a
hospital typically are not in the ICS. Orthopaedic surgeons should understand how an
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:55 PM

6/17

ICS is developed and executed and avenues for communication. They also can provide
input as to the resources that may be necessary to manage various types of disaster
events.
Preparation, rehearsal, and redundant communication systems are the hallmarks of an
effective disaster response that can withstand the inherent chaos of disasters. Regular
methods of communication may not work with power outages and potential cell tower
damage. Within the hospital, phone lines may be overwhelmed, necessitating alternate
communication methods, such as handheld devices or runners. Similarly, transportation
may be disrupted by roadway destruction or blockage. Providers must consider
alternatives.
Key components of the medical disaster response that the ICS will oversee are triage,
evacuation, and resource management. Orthopaedic surgeons must understand that
victims will be triaged into one of five categories and transported based on their triage
status.5
Minimal—Victims (walking wounded) are expected to survive injuries with or without
medical treatment.
Delayed—Management is required for injuries but can be safely delayed without
affecting survival.
Immediate—Injuries require immediate management to ensure good survivability.
Expectant—Victim is alive, but injuries provide little to no chance of survival given
current resources.
Dead—Fatality, no signs of life, no respiratory drive
Appropriate triage is critical in MCIs and disaster situations because the physical and
personnel resources are being used in a specific manner to provide the greatest care for
the greatest number of patients. For example, the over-triage of patients (ie, minimal
patients who are triaged immediately) makes it impossible to render critical care.
Similarly, if the hospital systems are flooded with walking wounded and are not following
triage guidelines, resources will be diverted from patients with immediate life-threating
injuries. Walking wounded blocking critically ill patients was observed after the 2017 Las

Vegas shooting.11 This is the crucial distinction between medical care during disasters
and routine situations.
As critically injured patients arrive at the hospital, orthopaedic surgeons will play a
critical role in their treatment. Born et al12 described the nuances of establishing an
orthopaedic chain of command, how to contact the team if a disaster is activated, and
how to effectively integrate an orthopaedic department’s resources into the hospital
response (Resource 4). All members of an orthopaedic department, either in an
academic or private setting, should have an idea of the role they may play in the event of
a disaster or MCI. Although orthopaedic surgeons will be needed during such events,
their role may not always involve performing orthopaedic surgeries or procedures.
Orthopaedic surgeons and other physicians, nurses, and healthcare providers must be
prepared to provide care in an area that is not their day-to-day expertise. Healthcare
team members’ flexibility is different from that of the all-hazards approach, which is
defined by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid services as an “integrated approach to
emergency preparedness planning that focuses on capacities and capabilities that are
critical to preparedness for a full spectrum of emergencies or disasters.”9 This approach
is critical to ensure that adequate healthcare providers are available to treat the critically
ill and get the healthcare system and community through various disaster situations.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, many orthopaedic residents worked shifts in other
departments to cover for physicians who needed a break or who were attending to
critically ill patients.13Table 2 lists resources on how orthopaedic surgeons who want to
be more involved in disaster situations at any level (local, national, or international) can
educate themselves and pursue these opportunities before disaster strikes.14

Disaster Response Considerations for Orthopaedic Surgeons
Protocols to manage disasters continue after the victim has arrived at the hospital.
Orthopaedic injuries may be a considerable portion of the injuries sustained.
Medical records are best kept electronically rather than in writing or verbally.
During and after the disaster response, providers must maintain an awareness of their own
and their team members’ personal safety and physical and mental well-being.

Disaster Response Considerations for Orthopaedic Surgeons
After victims of a disaster have been transported to the hospital, the disaster response
system continues but on a smaller scale from the MCI. Many hospitals have established
protocols, systems, and backup systems to manage patient influx. These systems often
are verified by The Joint Commission for Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations and
the American College of Surgeons via routine site visits and quality programs to ensure
established hospital/trauma protocols are followed and effective for providing high-
quality trauma care.15 In this phase, many orthopaedic surgeons will encounter the
injured for the first time. Teamwork between orthopaedic surgeons and other
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:55 PM
AAOS | Disaster and Mass Casualty Preparedness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000591
11/17

healthcare team members is important to ensure that preventable deaths are avoided
by triaging injuries across specialties and reducing clinical errors.16
Orthopaedic surgeons should expect a high proportion of orthopaedic injuries from
disasters, regardless of the type of disaster. For example, in the Paris terrorist attack in
2015, more than 50% of the injuries were orthopaedic in nature despite more than 80%
of the injuries being related to gunshot wounds.17 During earthquakes in developing
countries, research revealed that just less than 90% of the injuries sustained were
orthopaedic in nature, 65% of which were fractures.18 These examples demonstrate the
important role that orthopaedic surgeons play in the treatment of victims after a
disaster. Many factors may influence the type and timing of treatment orthopaedic
surgeons can initially provide.
Basic treatment options, such as antibiotic agents and tetanus boosters for open
fractures, fracture reduction, splinting, and skeletal traction should not be forgotten;
however, with an inundation of patients and limited resources, these basic treatment
options may require some form of improvisation. These actions may be performed in
different locations, such as the intensive care unit, and other materials (ie, pillows as
splints in lieu of plaster of Paris) may be necessary. Surgical treatment options for
orthopaedic injuries also may be altered or delayed because of operating room
availability and patient stability. For example, after the earthquakes in Pakistan and Haiti
in 2005 and 2010, respectively, orthopaedic surgeons relied on damage-control
orthopaedics, external fixation, and amputations for orthopaedic fractures, often in
tents and other temporary medical facilities, especially if the fracture was open in
nature.19,20 In normal circumstances—not disasters—these same fractures may be able
to be managed via definitive fixation or limb salvage. To treat earthquake victims,
external fixators often were placed without the use of fluoroscopy or without
sterilization of the entire limb, demonstrating the flexibility and reliance on anatomic
principles that orthopaedic surgeons must have. Substantial numbers of pediatric
casualties occurred in these events, highlighting the need for appropriate pediatric
supplies.
Regardless of the disaster type, orthopaedic surgeons should be ready to assist the team
in the management of orthopaedic injuries during disasters, and basic principles, such as
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:55 PM
AAOS | Disaster and Mass Casualty Preparedness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000591
12/17

antibiotic agents and damage-control orthopaedics must be used to help stabilize
patients. Ultimately, in a disaster situation, saving lives and providing the greatest good
for the greatest number of patients must be emphasized. Different treatment algorithms
from non-disaster situations must be implemented to provide optimal care for the
greatest number of patients. Flexible application of principles, teamwork, and resources
help overcome the challenges of MCIs.
Another important aspect of patient care is communication, specifically regarding
medical records. Many MCIs and hospital trauma protocols state how medical
documentation should occur during disaster scenarios. This is especially important
during MCIs because medical decisions acutely need to be made and tracked; however,
long-term patients also need this information to help them recover and obtain necessary
medical equipment, such as prosthetic limbs. Many MCIs are moving toward electronic
medical record tracking via mobile devices because of the improved ability to track a
victim’s status compared with paper records.21 Similar to paper records, verbal
communication is prone to medical errors in disaster situations. Therefore, sole use of
verbal communication should not be considered in the tracking and management of
patients during a disaster.22 If electronic records are not available, paper or digital
copies of the medical records can be stored.
Disaster response is inherently chaotic and stressful. These factors can be mitigated, but
not eliminated, by preparedness. Providers must maintain an awareness of their own
and their team members’ physical safety to avoid becoming a casualty. Fatigue and
dehydration can substantially degrade performance and should be avoided.
Tremendous psychologic stresses may occur, not only on casualties and their families
but also on the providers. Acknowledging this stress and providing counseling and other
relief mechanisms are important during response and recovery.
Summary
Regardless of the disaster type, orthopaedic surgeons play a critical role in the disaster
response.

13/17

Successful triage is a key component of disaster response and helps provide critical care to the
greatest number of patients.
Optimization of patient care during a disaster occurs with interdisciplinary teamwork and pre-
disaster preparation.
Under the all-hazards approach, healthcare team members, including orthopaedic surgeons,
may be called on to perform other healthcare duties outside their field of expertise.

Summary
Orthopaedic surgeons play a substantial role in disaster response. Disaster
preparedness consists of four phases (mitigation, preparation, response, and
rehabilitation), and practicing protocols and preparing before disaster strikes are
considered the best methods to minimize the effects of a disaster. A disaster becomes a
MCI if it generates more patients than a local system can handle via standard protocols.
Teamwork among orthopaedic surgeons and healthcare providers is important to avoid
preventable deaths and optimize patient care in resource-strained environments.
Because of a shortage of resources during a disaster, orthopaedic surgeons may be
called on to perform procedures in unusual places, use damage-control orthopaedic
principles and external fixation, or provide medical care outside their orthopaedic
specialty. Being a team player and understanding the basics behind disasters and
disaster response will enable the orthopaedic surgeon be a valuable member of the
disaster healthcare team.
